subject: How do you make residual plots to determine what is wrong with a model?

messages.author: c30c9e29d10d3cd7
messages.subject: How do you make residual plots to determine what is wrong with a model?
parts:
Hi all,

I am using unmarked to build and evaluate my model. I used parametric bootstrapping to evaluate model goodness-of-fit of the best model. However, my findings found that my model fit is not that great and my models are over dispersed (c-hat).

I wanted to check the residuals of my "best" model as i would a glm or glmm (i.e. plot it expected vs. observed values) to see if I can improve my model.

However, when i input the code below I get 6 columns one for each of my distance categories.

How does one plot the residuals from the unmarked output? So far I have not been able to find an example anywhere?

Thanks

Ingrid

umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y=as.matrix(yDat), siteCovs=covs, survey="line", dist.breaks=c(0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 500), tlength=covs$translength,  unitsIn="m")

fm<- distsamp (~1~ndvi+riv+I(ndvi^2)+lake+prec+dem+temp, umf, keyfun="hazard", output="density", unitsOut="kmsq")
fm

residual(fm)

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] How do you make residual plots to determine what is wrong with a model?
parts:
Dear Ingrid,

in a distance sampling (DS) analysis with binned distance such as you do in unmarked, you have a sort of multivariate analysis: at each site, you have multiple responses, corresponding to the counts in each distance category. So your residuals naturally have this 2-dimensional structure (site by distance class). You can then look where the model does not fit well (i.e., for which site and/or which distance class), by doing things like this (some code snippets from a DS analysis I did a while ago):

getY(umf)     # Observed counts

     dclass

dsite  0  1 2

   1   5  3 0


(fv <- fitted(fm4))     # Fitted values: expected counts

           [,1]       [,2]       [,3]

 [1,] 14.121756  9.9128722 2.12411574

 [2,]  1.222467  0.8581198 0.18387666


(raw.resi <- residuals(fm4))     # Raw residuals

     dclass

dsite           0           1           2

   1   -9.1217556 -6.91287219 -2.12411574

   2   -0.2224669  0.14188018 -0.18387666

   3   -7.1217556 -6.91287219 -2.12411574


(resi <- 100*(raw.resi / fv))     # Scaled residuals

     dclass

dsite           0            1           2

   1   -64.593637  -69.7363192 -100.000000

   2   -18.198196   16.5338423 -100.000000

   3   -50.431092  -69.7363192 -100.000000



# Comparison of observed data, fitted values and residuals

print(cbind(getY(umf), fv, raw.resi, resi), 1)

matplot(1:3, t(raw.resi), type = 'l', lty = 1, xlab = "Distance class")

lines(1:3, apply(t(raw.resi),1,mean), lwd = 3)

In this way, you can explore ways in which the observed data do not conform well to the expected data under the model (i.e., for which site and distance class the model does not fit well).

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Re: How do you make residual plots to determine what is wrong with a model?
parts:
Dear Ingrid,

it shows that the green site makes a big contribution to the lack of fit. At every distance class, and especially in classes 4 and 5, there are many more birds observed than what one would expect under the model. And similar for some of the other sites.

What these residuals allow you is to identify sites and/or distance classes that are "atypical" in the sense that the model does not fit well for them. Once you recognize some patterns in there, there are broadly two avenues that you could go:
(1) Eliminate some sites and call them outliers. Generally, this is not a good approach, because it bears the serious risk of tailoring your data to the model. But in exceptional cases you may have one or a few such extreme sites and can perhaps come up with an explanation for why their data are exceptional (perhaps because some over-eager field assistant was at these sites ?) and this may warrant their exclusion. --- Another approach may be to express the fit only for the remaining sites and if this leads to an acceptable GOF test statistic accept that the model fits for most if not all sites ?
(2) But the best approach might be to expand your model by adding into it additional structure that accounts for the remaining, non-random patterns that were picked up by the GOF test. For this you can ask yourself what factors may explain positive (or negative) residuals of some sites or for some distance classes and then try to add into the model covariates that account for that. Or you could simply account for more variability in site-specific abundance than what the Poisson allows, i.e., by assuming a NegBin distribution for abundance.

Some of these model expansions might make it necessary for you to go down the BUGS avenue; see chapters 8 and 9 in the AHM1 book.

Best regards --  Marc

I see now that in the help text for that function this is only shown as a note further down:

 

Note:

 

     If you aren't interested in estimating phi, but you want to use

     the negative binomial distribution, simply set numPrimary=1 when

     formatting the data.

What these residuals allow you is to identify sites and/or distance classes that are "atypical" in the sense that the model does not fit well for them. Once you recognize some patterns in there, there are broadly two avenues that you could go:
(1) Eliminate some sites and call them outliers. Generally, this is not a good approach, because it bears the serious risk of tailoring your data to the model. But in exceptional cases you may have one or a few such extreme sites and can perhaps come up with an explanation for why their data are exceptional (perhaps because some over-eager field assistant was at these sites ?) and this may warrant their exclusion. --- Another approach may be to express the fit only for the remaining sites and if this leads to an acceptable GOF test statistic accept that the model fits for most if not all sites ?
(2) But the best approach might be to expand your model by adding into it additional structure that accounts for the remaining, non-random patterns that were picked up by the GOF test. For this you can ask yourself what factors may explain positive (or negative) residuals of some sites or for some distance classes and then try to add into the model covariates that account for that. Or you could simply account for more variability in site-specific abundance than what the Poisson allows, i.e., by assuming a NegBin distribution for abundance.

Some of these model expansions might make it necessary for you to go down the BUGS avenue; see chapters 8 and 9 in the AHM1 book.

Best regards --  Marc
